page3_img_1.png.title: Side-by-side comparison of original table DiffViewer and redesigned block-based DiffViewer
page3_img_1.png.description: The figure shows two screenshots comparing the original DiffViewer (left) and the redesigned UI (right). The left image is a white, table-style listing of diffs with columns for Count, Comments, Owners, Category, Description and a red-highlighted row to indicate a selected/high-priority diff. The right (dark-themed) redesign is annotated with four callouts: (1) a top progress bar and build identifier (shown as “Build 2.1.19343.1” with progress 1/15), (2) a left control panel for view, clustering and block-size controls, (3) a central tiled/block area where individual diff cards show description text, counts, predicted status (e.g., “New Feature”), flag and Logs buttons, and (4) a right detail panel containing a Diff description, count, an AI-generated summary, status, and comment area. Together the images illustrate the paper’s key UI changes: moving from a dense, linear table to a consolidated, block-based layout that surfaces LLM predictions, summaries, flags, and clustering controls to reduce navigation and manual inspection.

page7_img_1.png.title: Survey table of top challenges and evaluated DiffViewer features
page7_img_1.png.description: A two-part table summarizing the survey items shown to on-call engineers: the left column labels the survey category and the right column lists specific items. The first block, “Biggest Challenges,” (to be ranked from most to least challenging) lists nine pain points such as difficulty finding a specific diff, finding a previously worked-on diff, jumping between screens when diagnosing a diff, assigning a diff to the correct owner, re-establishing context between diffs, writing summaries for owners, time to manually label predictable diffs, estimating work progress, and other unspecified challenges. The second block, “Feature Evaluation,” (assessed on a 5‑point Likert scale from Not‑Likely to Very‑Likely) enumerates candidate improvements: label predictions for review, a progress bar, AI summaries in the detail panel, flagging diffs, alternative views (e.g., by count or cluster), clustering diffs, a tile layout for diffs, and placing the detail panel on the right. The table documents the specific challenges and prototype features the study used to collect rankings and likelihood-of-adoption ratings.

page9_img_1.png.title: Survey: Likelihood of Adopting New DiffViewer Features
page9_img_1.png.description: A horizontal stacked bar chart titled “New Features Likelihood of Usage” reports survey percentages for eight proposed DiffViewer features (rows list features such as Diffs in tile layout; Clustering diffs; AI Summaries in the Detail Panel; Detail panel on the right; Progress bar; Label predictions generated for your review; Flagging Diffs; and Other views). Color encodes adoption sentiment from red (least likely) through gray (neutral) to dark green (most likely). The chart shows strong positive responses (large green segments, roughly 60–80% of ratings) for Other views, Flagging Diffs, Label predictions, and the Progress bar, indicating these are the most likely to be adopted. Clustering diffs and the right-side detail panel received mixed but generally positive/neutral ratings, while AI Summaries has a notable orange/red left segment (some respondents least likely to adopt) alongside a moderate green segment, signifying mixed opinions about that feature.

page8_img_1.png.title: Heatmap of Ranked On‑Call Diff‑Labeling Challenges
page8_img_1.png.description: A heatmap showing how five on‑call engineers ranked ten common challenges (y‑axis) during Diff labeling; each column is a participant and cell values (and color scale) indicate rank 1 (dark green, most impactful) to 10 (pale, least). Tasks like “Jumping Between Screens” (ranks 1,2,3,5,6) and “Finding a Diff You Were Working On” (2,4,4,5,5) are consistently ranked among the top pain points. Other items show more disagreement across participants — for example, “Difficulty Finding a Specific Diff” was ranked 1 by two participants but 6–9 by others — while tasks such as “Writing Summaries When Assigning Diffs” and estimating remaining/total work tended to receive higher (less urgent) ranks. Overall the figure highlights navigation and re-finding diffs as the most common, regularly high‑priority issues.
